metaDesc: A family-friendly Koh Chang itinerary in Thailand: calm-water beaches, Klong Plu Waterfall kids can swim in, and easy island snorkelling. A relaxed 3-day, 2-night day-by-day plan with real prices and honest warnings about the steep island road.

h1:
Koh Chang For Families
Calm Beaches, Waterfall & Snorkelling
intro: Taking the kids (or grandparents) to Koh Chang doesn't have to be a slog. The island has calm-water beaches where little ones can play in the sand, Klong Plu Waterfall that's an easy walk with a pool you can wade into, and snorkelling boat trips around the nearby islands that older kids can handle comfortably. We've laid this out as a relaxed 3-day, 2-night plan with room for naps, plus the real prices and the spots where you'll want to be extra careful — especially the steep, hairpin road that loops the island.

blocks.html: Koh Chang is Thailand's second-largest island, part of the Mu Ko Chang National Park in Trat province. The west coast is the side that works best for families: long beaches, water that's fairly calm during high season, and a mix of restaurants and resorts at every price level. The waterfall and the snorkelling boat trips aren't far either — you can drive or hop on a songthaew (shared pickup truck) to reach them. This plan is paced to match a kid's rhythm, without cramming in so much that everyone ends up exhausted.

blocks.text: Why Koh Chang works for families

items: Calm water in high season — Klong Prao and Kai Bae on the west coast stay gentle from November to April, so kids can build sandcastles and paddle in the shallows.
An easy walk to the waterfall — Klong Plu Waterfall is about a 1 km walk from the car park, on a fairly flat path with rest stops along the way. Kids and older relatives can manage it.
You can choose how quiet you want it — for real quiet, head to the southern end of Klong Prao or out toward Ban Salak Phet; for shops and restaurants, stick to Kai Bae.
Snorkelling without being a strong swimmer — the boat trips stop at shallow spots where you can wear a life jacket, so older kids who can swim a bit can get in with their parents.

blocks.title: When to go
blocks.html: Families should aim for the high season, roughly November to April: clear water, calm seas, and snorkelling boat trips running every day. The monsoon months from May to October bring heavy rain and rough seas, the boat trips usually get cancelled, and some smaller resorts close for the stretch. If you have to go during the rainy season, always check with your accommodation before booking.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Arrive on the island + calm beach

items.activity: Drive or take a bus to Ao Thammachat pier, then board the car ferry across to Ao Sapparot pier.
items.note: The ferry carries cars and the crossing takes about 30 minutes. The main route now runs Ao Thammachat–Ao Sapparot; the old Centre Point pier has stopped operating.

items.activity: Get onto the island, take a songthaew or drive yourself to check in around Klong Prao or Kai Bae beach.
items.note: A songthaew from the pier to White Sand Beach / Kai Bae runs about 60–120 THB per person. Always agree the price before you get in.

items.activity: Rest up, let the kids nap, then head down for a swim on the beach in front of your place once the sun softens.
items.note: Klong Prao Beach runs more than 3 km, with fairly shallow, calm water in high season — good for kids playing in the sand.

items.activity: Watch the sunset from the beach, then find an easy-going beachfront restaurant for dinner.
items.note: The west coast gives you a clear sunset over the sea. Pick a restaurant with high chairs or room for kids to walk around.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Klong Plu Waterfall + quiet beach

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Morning at the waterfall, chilled-out beach afternoon

items.activity: Head to Klong Plu Waterfall (also spelled Khlong Phlu) early, walking in about 1 km to reach the falls.
items.note: National park entry for Thais is 40 THB for adults and 20 THB for children (foreigners pay 200 for adults, 100 for children). One ticket also gets you into Than Mayom Waterfall on the same day.

items.activity: Wade into the pool below the falls, let the kids play in the shallow part while parents stay close.
items.note: The pool is fairly deep and the rocks are slippery, so put kids in a life jacket or float ring, don't let them play alone, and don't climb up to the top of the falls — it's dangerous and the path up has been closed.

items.activity: Head back to your place for a midday break, then in the late afternoon go to a quieter beach, such as the southern end of Klong Prao or Bang Bao Beach.
items.note: If you want the quietest spot, the Ban Salak Phet–Long Beach area in the southeast is very quiet, but it's far and you'll need to drive yourself.

items.activity: Seafood dinner at Bang Bao village, then a stroll along the wooden pier to watch the fishing boats.
items.note: Bang Bao is an old fishing village with waterfront seafood restaurants — a relaxed spot that's nice for walking with kids.

blocks.text: Day 3 — Snorkelling around the islands + heading home

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: Snorkelling boat trip, then the trip back

items.activity: Join a snorkelling boat trip from Bang Bao pier, stopping to swim around the nearby islands like Koh Yak, Koh Wai, and the reefs at Koh Rang.
items.note: A full-day wooden-boat trip is around 700 THB per person (kids are often half price), plus about 200 THB for the park fee. Speedboat tours cost more, starting around 900–1,200 THB.

items.activity: Swim and look at the coral at the shallow spots, keep kids in life jackets the whole time, and take photos on the boat.
items.note: Pick the shallow spots the guide recommends. Keep non-swimming kids near their parents and in a life jacket, and don't push it if a child is scared of deep water.

items.activity: Lunch on the boat or on an island, then the boat brings you back to shore in the afternoon.
items.note: Always check the forecast the night before. If the sea is rough or it's pouring, the trip may be cancelled — keep your plan flexible.

items.activity: Pack up, check out, take a songthaew to the pier, and catch the ferry back to the mainland.
items.note: Leave plenty of extra time for the ferry and songthaew waits, especially on long weekends when it's busy.

items.name: Klong Prao Beach
items.blurb: A beach running more than 3 km with shallow, calm water in high season and resorts at every price level — good for kids in the sand and parents relaxing.

items.name: Kai Bae Beach
items.blurb: Plenty of restaurants and places to eat, with fairly calm water at both ends of the beach — a mix of convenience and family-friendliness.

items.name: Bang Bao – southern Klong Prao
items.blurb: Quieter than the main beaches with fewer people — good if you want to escape the bustle. You can take the kids for a walk along the Bang Bao wooden pier.

blocks.title: The sea and your kids
blocks.html: The west-coast beaches are calm in high season, but during the monsoon the waves pick up and there may be warning flags. Always check the signs and flag colours before getting in. At low tide some stretches get very shallow and you can walk far out — a good time to hunt for shells with the kids in the morning.

blocks.text: The warnings we'll give you straight

blocks.html: Koh Chang really is a fun trip, but there are a few things families need to watch out for. We'd rather tell you straight than let you find out the hard way.

items: The island road is steep with hairpin bends — especially on the way to the southern beaches, where it gets very steep with tight corners. If you're driving yourself, use a low gear going downhill and brake in bursts. A motorbike is even more dangerous; if you're not used to the roads, don't force it — a songthaew is safer.
Snorkelling boats depend on the weather — during the monsoon the sea is rough and trips often get cancelled. Always check the forecast, and don't force a boat trip if the sea is up.
Some places close in low season — certain resorts and small shops shut down for the May–October stretch. If you're going in the rainy season, confirm with your accommodation before booking.
The waterfall rocks are slippery — the pool below Klong Plu Waterfall has slippery rocks, so kids need a life jacket and an adult watching close by. Never climb to the top of the falls.
Build in extra travel time — the ferry and songthaews can mean long waits, and long weekends get crowded. Leave enough buffer so you're not stressed with the kids.
Life jackets / float rings for the kids (some spots lend them out, but bringing your own is reassuring).
Sunscreen and hats — the island sun is strong, especially on the boat.
Shoes you can wade in, for both the waterfall and the rocky parts of some beaches.
A basic medicine kit, kids' motion-sickness tablets, and insect repellent for the waterfall trail.
Cash — small shops and some songthaews don't take transfers or cards.

faq.q: Is Koh Chang suitable for young kids?
faq.a: Yes, if you go during high season (November–April), because the west-coast beaches like Klong Prao and Kai Bae stay calm, so kids can play in the sand and paddle in the shallows. Klong Plu Waterfall is an easy walk too. Just watch out for the steep island road and the slippery rocks at the waterfall, and keep a close eye on kids throughout.

faq.q: Can you swim at Klong Plu Waterfall, and can kids get in?
faq.a: You can swim in the pool below the falls. It's about a 1 km walk from the car park on a path that isn't too steep. Kids can play in the shallow part, but they should wear a life jacket because the pool is fairly deep and the rocks are slippery. Don't climb to the top of the falls — it's dangerous and the path up has been closed.

faq.q: Can kids go snorkelling at Koh Chang, and what does it cost?
faq.a: Older kids who can handle a boat can go. The trips stop at shallow spots where they can wear a life jacket and play with their parents. A full-day wooden-boat trip is around 700 THB per person, with kids often at half price, plus about 200 THB for the park fee. Speedboat tours cost more, starting around 900–1,200 THB. During the monsoon, trips are usually cancelled because of rough seas.

faq.q: How many days is enough for a family on Koh Chang?
faq.a: 3 days and 2 nights is about right — not too rushed, with time to enjoy the beach, spend a day at the waterfall, and do a snorkelling trip another day, plus room for kids' naps and travel. If you're really short on time, 2 days and 1 night is enough for the beach and the waterfall.

faq.q: Is it dangerous to drive yourself on Koh Chang?
faq.a: The island road is very steep with sharp hairpin bends, especially heading to the southern beaches. If you're not used to the roads, we don't recommend riding a motorbike. In a car you'll need a low gear going downhill and to brake in bursts. For families with kids, a songthaew is safer and less stressful.
